entry.title: Two Envelopes with a Uniform Prior

link.title: Two Envelopes with a Uniform Prior

entry.content:
Problem.

Let $X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,100)$. Two envelopes contain $X$ dollars and $2X$ dollars. You choose an envelope, and open it to observe its amount. You may then keep it or switch to the other envelope. What strategy maximizes the probability of ending with the larger amount, and what is this probability? Does the same strategy maximize the expected amount received?

Solution.

Write $Y$ for the observed amount and $Z$ for the amount in the other envelope. Let $S$ be the event that the selected envelope is the smaller one, so $Y=X$ and $Z=2X$, and let $L$ be the event that it is the larger one, so $Y=2X$ and $Z=X$. Before observing $Y$, both events have probability $1/2$.

1. Update the probabilities after seeing the amount

If $100<Y<200$, the selected envelope must be the larger one: the smaller amount $X$ never exceeds $100$. Keeping it wins with certainty.

If $0<Y<100$, either envelope could have been selected. The conditional densities are

\[f_{Y\mid S}(y)=\frac1{100},\qquad f_{Y\mid L}(y)=\frac1{200}, \qquad 0<y<100.\]

The second density is smaller because $Y=2X$ spreads the same probability mass over an interval twice as long. Since $Y$ is continuous, we use these densities in Bayes’ formula:

\[\mathbb P(S\mid Y=y) =\frac{\frac12\cdot\frac1{100}} {\frac12\cdot\frac1{100}+\frac12\cdot\frac1{200}} =\frac23, \qquad \mathbb P(L\mid Y=y)=\frac13.\]

Equivalently, observing an amount in a short interval $[y,y+\mathrm{d}y]$ corresponds to an interval of width $\mathrm{d}y$ for $X$ if the smaller envelope was selected, but only width $\mathrm{d}y/2$ if the larger envelope was selected. The two explanations therefore have probability ratio $2:1$.

2. Choose the action with the higher winning probability

For $0<y<100$, switching wins exactly when the selected envelope is the smaller one, with conditional probability $2/3$; keeping wins with probability $1/3$. For $100<y<200$, keeping wins with certainty. Thus an optimal strategy is

\[\boxed{ \text{Switch if }Y\leq100;\qquad \text{keep if }Y>100. }\]

The observation $Y=100$ has probability zero, so the action at this boundary does not affect the overall result. Comparing the two actions at each observed amount establishes optimality; randomizing between them cannot improve the conditional winning probability.

To calculate the overall winning probability, condition on which envelope was initially selected. If we selected $X$, then $Y=X\leq100$ and we always switch to $2X$. If we selected $2X$, we keep the larger envelope exactly when $2X>100$, or $X>50$. Therefore

\[\boxed{ \mathbb P(\text{finish with }2X) =\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\mathbb P(X>50) =\frac12+\frac12\cdot\frac12 =\frac34. }\]

3. Maximize the expected amount

For $0<y<100$, the other envelope contains $2y$ with posterior probability $2/3$ and $y/2$ with probability $1/3$. Hence

\[\mathbb E[Z\mid Y=y] =\frac23(2y)+\frac13\left(\frac y2\right) =\frac32y>y.\]

For $100<y<200$, the other envelope certainly contains $y/2<y$. Thus the same strategy also maximizes expected dollars received.

Let $V$ be the final amount under this strategy. Conditional on initially selecting the smaller envelope, $V=2X$. Conditional on initially selecting the larger envelope, $V=X$ when $X\leq50$ and $V=2X$ when $X>50$. Consequently,

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[V] &=\frac12\mathbb E[2X] +\frac12\left( \int_0^{50}\frac{x}{100}\,\mathrm{d}x +\int_{50}^{100}\frac{2x}{100}\,\mathrm{d}x \right)\\ &=50+\frac12(12.5+75) =\boxed{93.75\text{ dollars}}. \end{aligned}\]

For comparison, always keeping or always switching gives expected amount $\frac12\mathbb E[X]+\frac12\mathbb E[2X]=75$ dollars. Observing the amount and acting on it raises the expectation by $18.75$ dollars.

entry.title: HTH Before HHT – A Pattern Race

link.title: HTH Before HHT – A Pattern Race

entry.content:
Problem.

A fair coin is tossed independently. What is the probability that $HTH$ appears as three consecutive outcomes before $HHT$ does?

Solution.

Let $\tau_{HTH}$ and $\tau_{HHT}$ be the numbers of tosses needed for the first complete occurrences of the respective patterns. Define

\[W:=\{\tau_{HTH}<\tau_{HHT}\}, \qquad p:=\mathbb P(W).\]

Method 1. Restart after an unsuccessful attempt

Ignore any initial tails and wait for the first head. Neither pattern can appear before this head, so the probability of eventually winning from this point is still $p$.

Starting from this first $H$, there are three possibilities:

  • The next toss is $H$, with probability $1/2$. Once the sequence ends in $HH$, every additional head preserves that suffix, and the first subsequent tail completes $HHT$. Thus $HTH$ cannot win along this branch.
  • The next two tosses are $TH$, with probability $1/4$. They complete $HTH$, so we win immediately.
  • The next two tosses are $TT$, with probability $1/4$. The sequence ends in $HTT$, neither target has appeared, and no nonempty suffix is a beginning of either target. We therefore start afresh, with winning probability $p$.

By conditioning on these three possibilities,

\[p=\frac12\cdot0+\frac14\cdot1+\frac14p.\]

Consequently,

\[\boxed{\mathbb P(\tau_{HTH}<\tau_{HHT})=p=\frac13.}\]

Method 2. Conditional probabilities given initial tosses

Use $\mathbb P(W\mid H)$ to mean the probability of $W$ conditional on the first toss being $H$; similarly, $\mathbb P(W\mid HT)$ conditions on the first two tosses being $HT$. These conditions specify the initial prefix of the sequence.

Conditioning on the first toss gives

\[p=\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid H)+\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid T).\]

An initial tail contributes no progress toward either pattern, and subsequent tosses are independent of it. Hence

\[\mathbb P(W\mid T)=p, \qquad \mathbb P(W\mid H)=p.\]

Next, condition on the second toss:

\[\mathbb P(W\mid H) =\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HH) +\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HT).\]

As in Method 1, an initial $HH$ guarantees that $HHT$ wins when the first tail arrives, so

\[\mathbb P(W\mid HH)=0.\]

After an initial $HT$, a head wins immediately, while a tail leaves $HTT$ and restarts the race. Therefore

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb P(W\mid HT) &=\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HTH) +\frac12\mathbb P(W\mid HTT)\\ &=\frac12+\frac12p. \end{aligned}\]

Combining the equations,

\[p=\frac12\left(\frac12+\frac12p\right) =\frac14+\frac14p,\]

which again yields $p=1/3$.

Remark.

Equal probabilities in a fixed window do not imply equal winning probabilities. Each pattern has probability $1/8$ in any specified block of three tosses. However, the race examines overlapping windows and stops at the first occurrence. The patterns interact differently with their partial matches: reaching $HH$ guarantees an eventual $HHT$ win, whereas reaching $HT$ still allows the race to restart. Thus the race is asymmetric, with

\[\mathbb P(\tau_{HTH}<\tau_{HHT})=\frac13, \qquad \mathbb P(\tau_{HHT}<\tau_{HTH})=\frac23.\]

The related poster HHT Before HTH – A Conditional Waiting Time asks for the expected stopping time conditional on $HHT$ winning. This problem instead asks for the probability that $HTH$ wins. The same prefix transitions support both calculations, but the quantities being computed are different.

entry.title: A Mathematical Review of Linear Regression

link.title: A Mathematical Review of Linear Regression

entry.content:
Linear regression has three distinct layers: least squares is an optimization problem, projection explains its geometry, and assumptions on the errors justify statistical inference.

1. Model, notation, and assumptions

With $n$ observations and $d$ coefficients, including the intercept, write

\[\mathbf y=X oldsymbol eta+ oldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad X=[\,\mathbf 1_n\ \ \widetilde X\,]\in\mathbb R^{n imes d}, \qquad oldsymbol eta= egin{pmatrix} eta_0\\widetilde{ oldsymbol eta}\end{pmatrix} = igl( eta_0,\widetilde{ oldsymbol eta}^{ op} igr)^{ op}.\]

The predictor vector $\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i\in\mathbb R^{d-1}$ is a column vector; the $i$th row of $\widetilde X$ is $\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i^{ op}$. Thus

\[y_i= eta_0+\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i^{ op}\widetilde{ oldsymbol eta}+\varepsilon_i.\]

Unless stated otherwise, assume $\operatorname{rank}(X)=d<n$ and condition on $X$. Least-squares algebra needs no distributional assumptions. The classical moment assumptions are

\[\mathbb E[ oldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]=\mathbf0, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}( oldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma^2I_n, \qquad \sigma^2>0.\]

These give unbiasedness and the usual sampling covariance. Equal variances and zero correlations alone do not imply independence. Exact finite-sample $t$ and $F$ inference uses the stronger Gaussian assumption

\[ oldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X\sim N(\mathbf0,\sigma^2I_n).\]

2. OLS and projection geometry

Ordinary least squares (OLS) minimizes $Q(\mathbf b)=|\mathbf y-X\mathbf b|_2^2$. Its first-order condition (FOC) gives

\[ abla Q(\mathbf b)=-2X^{ op}\mathbf y+2X^{ op}X\mathbf b, \qquad X^{ op}X\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}=X^{ op}\mathbf y.\]

Full column rank makes $X^{ op}X$ positive definite because $\mathbf a^{ op}X^{ op}X\mathbf a=|X\mathbf a|^2>0$ for every nonzero $\mathbf a$. Hence

\[ oxed{\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}=(X^{ op}X)^{-1}X^{ op}\mathbf y}, \qquad \widehat{\mathbf y}=H\mathbf y, \qquad \mathbf e=M\mathbf y,\]

where

\[H=X(X^{ op}X)^{-1}X^{ op}, \qquad M=I_n-H, \qquad H^{ op}=H, \qquad H^2=H, \qquad HM=0.\]

The fitted vector is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf y$ onto the column space $\mathcal C(X)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. The residual lies in $\mathcal C(X)^\perp=\ker(X^{ op})$, so $X^{ op}\mathbf e=\mathbf0$. The row space and $\ker(X)$ instead live in coefficient space $\mathbb R^d$; a displacement in $\ker(X)$ leaves the fitted vector unchanged.

The Pythagorean identity gives both the minimization property and a useful expansion:

\[Q(\mathbf b) =\underbrace{\|\mathbf e\|^2}_{\mathrm{SSE}} +(\mathbf b-\widehat{ oldsymbol eta})^{ op} X^{ op}X(\mathbf b-\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}).\]

3. The intercept, sums of squares, and $R^2$

The intercept FOC is a particular coordinate of the normal equations:

\[0=\left. rac{\partial Q}{\partial eta_0} ight|_{\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}} =-2\sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i-\widehat eta_0-\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i^{ op}\widehat{\widetilde{ oldsymbol eta}} ight) =-2\sum_{i=1}^n e_i.\]

Consequently,

\[\sum_i e_i=0, \qquad \overline{\widehat y}= ar y, \qquad \widehat eta_0= ar y-\overline{\widetilde{\mathbf x}}^{ op}\widehat{\widetilde{ oldsymbol eta}}, \qquad \overline{\widetilde{\mathbf x}}= rac1n\sum_i\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i.\]

Define SSE (Sum of Squared Errors), TSS (Total Sum of Squares), and SSR (Regression Sum of Squares) by

\[\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2, \qquad \mathrm{TSS}=\sum_i(y_i- ar y)^2, \qquad \mathrm{SSR}=\sum_i(\widehat y_i- ar y)^2.\]

Some references use SSR for residual variation; here it always means explained variation. Since $\widehat{\mathbf y}- ar y\mathbf1_n\in\mathcal C(X)$ and $\mathbf e\perp\mathcal C(X)$,

\[\mathbf y- ar y\mathbf1_n =(\widehat{\mathbf y}- ar y\mathbf1_n)+\mathbf e \quad\Longrightarrow\quad oxed{\mathrm{TSS}=\mathrm{SSR}+\mathrm{SSE}}.\]

For a nonconstant response,

\[R^2=1- rac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{TSS}} = rac{\mathrm{SSR}}{\mathrm{TSS}}, \qquad \overline R^2 =1- rac{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-d)}{\mathrm{TSS}/(n-1)} =1- rac{n-1}{n-d}(1-R^2).\]

Adding predictor columns cannot increase the minimized SSE, so ordinary $R^2$ cannot decrease; adjusted $R^2$ can decrease and may be negative. Neither measures performance on new data. Without an intercept, the centered decomposition need not hold; if $\mathrm{TSS}=0$, centered $R^2$ is undefined.

4. Sampling covariance and residual degrees of freedom

Let $C=(X^{ op}X)^{-1}$. Substitution of the model yields

\[\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}- oldsymbol eta=CX^{ op} oldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad \mathbb E[\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}\mid X]= oldsymbol eta, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}\mid X) =CX^{ op}(\sigma^2I_n)XC =\sigma^2C.\]

Because $MX=0$, the residual is $\mathbf e=M oldsymbol\varepsilon$. The residual projection has rank and trace $n-d$, giving

\[\mathbb E[\mathrm{SSE}\mid X] =\mathbb E[ oldsymbol\varepsilon^{ op}M oldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X] =\operatorname{tr}\!\left(M\mathbb E[ oldsymbol\varepsilon oldsymbol\varepsilon^{ op}\mid X] ight) =\sigma^2(n-d).\]

Thus fitting a $d$-dimensional mean leaves $ u=n-d$ residual degrees of freedom, and

\[ oxed{s^2= rac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-d}}, \qquad \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}\mid X)=s^2C, \qquad \widehat{\operatorname{se}}(\widehat eta_j)=s\sqrt{C_{jj}}.\]

Under the moment assumptions, OLS is also the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov). Indeed, any other linear unbiased estimator has matrix $CX^{ op}+D$ with $DX=0$; its covariance exceeds that of OLS by the positive semidefinite matrix $\sigma^2DD^{ op}$.

If the conditional error covariance is instead $\Omega$, unbiasedness still follows from the zero conditional mean, but the covariance becomes $CX^{ op}\Omega XC$. The classical $s^2C$ formula then generally fails; heteroskedasticity or dependence requires an appropriate covariance estimator.

5. Exact coefficient $t$ tests and confidence intervals

Under Gaussian errors,

\[\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}\mid X\sim N( oldsymbol eta,\sigma^2C), \qquad rac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_ u, \qquad \widehat{ oldsymbol eta}\ \perp\!\!\!\perp\ \mathrm{SSE}\mid X.\]

An orthonormal basis of the residual space expresses $\mathrm{SSE}/\sigma^2$ as $ u$ independent squared standard normals. Independence follows because the coefficient error and residual are jointly Gaussian with zero cross-covariance, $\sigma^2CX^{ op}M=0$.

For $H_0: eta_j= eta_{j,0}$,

\[ oxed{t_j= rac{\widehat eta_j- eta_{j,0}}{s\sqrt{C_{jj}}}\sim t_ u\quad ext{under }H_0}.\]

Writing $T_ u$ for the Student $t$ CDF, the two-sided $p$ value and a $1-\alpha$ confidence interval are

\[p_j=2 igl[1-T_ u(|t_j|) igr], \qquad \widehat eta_j\ \pm\ t_{ u,1-\alpha/2}s\sqrt{C_{jj}}.\]

These are exact conditional results under Gaussian errors. Moment assumptions alone do not produce an exact $t$ distribution; asymptotic inference needs additional conditions. The same construction applies to a nonzero contrast $\mathbf a^{ op} oldsymbol eta$, replacing $\widehat eta_j$ and $C_{jj}$ by $\mathbf a^{ op}\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}$ and $\mathbf a^{ op}C\mathbf a$.

6. General linear restrictions and the $F$ test

Consider $H_0:A oldsymbol eta=\mathbf b$, where $A\in\mathbb R^{q imes d}$ has rank $q$. Let $\mathrm{SSE}_R$ and $\mathrm{SSE}_U$ be the restricted and unrestricted minima. With $ oldsymbol\delta=A\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}-\mathbf b$, minimizing the quadratic expansion of $Q$ subject to the restriction gives

\[\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}_R =\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}-CA^{ op}(ACA^{ op})^{-1} oldsymbol\delta, \qquad \mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_U = oldsymbol\delta^{ op}(ACA^{ op})^{-1} oldsymbol\delta.\]

Therefore, under the Gaussian model and $H_0$,

\[ oxed{ F= rac{(\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_U)/q}{\mathrm{SSE}_U/(n-d)} = rac{ oldsymbol\delta^{ op}(ACA^{ op})^{-1} oldsymbol\delta}{q\,s^2} \sim F_{q,n-d}. }\]

The increase $(\mathrm{SSE}R-\mathrm{SSE}_U)/\sigma^2$ is $\chi^2_q$: it measures noise along the $q$ fitted directions removed by the restriction. It is independent of the residual $\chi^2{n-d}$. If $G_{q,n-d}$ is the $F$ CDF, the $p$ value is $1-G_{q,n-d}(F_{\mathrm{obs}})$, with no factor of two. For a single restriction,

\[ oxed{F=t^2},\]

so its $F$ test and corresponding two-sided $t$ test have identical $p$ values.

7. Testing every coefficient versus testing every slope

For $H_0: oldsymbol eta=\mathbf0$, including the intercept, the restricted fit is zero. Hence $q=d$, $\mathrm{SSE}_R=\mathbf y^{ op}\mathbf y$, and

\[F_{\mathrm{all}} = rac{\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}^{ op}X^{ op}X\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}}{d\,s^2} = rac{\|\widehat{\mathbf y}\|^2}{d\,s^2} \sim F_{d,n-d}\quad ext{under }H_0.\]

The usual overall regression test instead leaves the intercept unrestricted and tests $H_0:\widetilde{ oldsymbol eta}=\mathbf0$, with $d\ge2$. The restricted fit is $ ar y\mathbf1_n$, so $q=d-1$ and $\mathrm{SSE}_R=\mathrm{TSS}$. Thus

\[ oxed{ F_{\mathrm{slopes}} = rac{\mathrm{SSR}/(d-1)}{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-d)} = rac{R^2/(d-1)}{(1-R^2)/(n-d)} \sim F_{d-1,n-d}\quad ext{under }H_0. }\]

The distinction is $|\widehat{\mathbf y}|^2=\mathrm{SSR}+n ar y^2$: the full-vector test also includes the fitted mean level. Centered $R^2$ alone determines the slopes test, not the full-vector test. Rejection of either joint null means at least one relevant coefficient is nonzero; it does not mean all are nonzero. Even under zero true slopes, fitting noise usually gives positive sample $R^2$.

8. Rank deficiency, pseudoinverses, and estimability

Now allow $\operatorname{rank}(X)=r<d$. The normal equations still hold, but $X^{ op}X$ is singular. If $X^+$ denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, all OLS solutions are

\[\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}=X^+\mathbf y+\mathbf h, \qquad \mathbf h\in\ker(X).\]

The choice $\mathbf h=\mathbf0$ uniquely minimizes the coefficient norm. Every solution nevertheless gives the same projection $\widehat{\mathbf y}=XX^+\mathbf y$, residuals, and SSE. Residual degrees of freedom are $n-r$, the dimension of the residual space, rather than the nominal $n-d$.

A contrast is estimable precisely when it is unchanged along every unidentified coefficient direction:

\[ oxed{ \mathbf a^{ op} oldsymbol eta ext{ is estimable} \iff \mathbf a\perp\ker(X) \iff \mathbf a\in\mathcal C(X^{ op}). }\]

Necessity follows because $ oldsymbol eta$ and $ oldsymbol eta+\mathbf h$ have the same mean whenever $X\mathbf h=0$. For sufficiency, write $\mathbf a=X^{ op}\mathbf u$; then $\mathbf u^{ op}\mathbf y$ is unbiased for $\mathbf a^{ op} oldsymbol eta$. The OLS contrast estimator has

\[\widehat L=\mathbf a^{ op}X^+\mathbf y, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat L\mid X) =\sigma^2\mathbf a^{ op}(X^{ op}X)^+\mathbf a.\]

For a nonzero estimable contrast, Gaussian errors, and $n>r$, replace $\sigma^2$ by $\mathrm{SSE}/(n-r)$ to obtain an exact $t_{n-r}$ test. A pseudoinverse chooses a coefficient representation; it does not make unidentified individual coefficients estimable.

9. Prediction and regularization

For a new predictor column $\mathbf x_0=(1,\widetilde{\mathbf x}_0^{ op})^{ op}$ in the full-rank model, the estimated conditional mean is $\widehat\mu_0=\mathbf x_0^{ op}\widehat{ oldsymbol eta}$. Under the Gaussian model, a confidence interval for the mean and a prediction interval for an independent new response with error variance $\sigma^2$ are, respectively,

\[\widehat\mu_0\ \pm\ t_{ u,1-\alpha/2}s\sqrt{\mathbf x_0^{ op}C\mathbf x_0}, \qquad \widehat\mu_0\ \pm\ t_{ u,1-\alpha/2}s\sqrt{1+\mathbf x_0^{ op}C\mathbf x_0}.\]

The extra $1$ accounts for the new observation’s noise. In a rank-deficient model, the new mean is estimable only if $\mathbf x_0$ belongs to the row space of $X$.

Ridge and lasso change the optimization problem by penalizing coefficients. With an unpenalized intercept and $D=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,1)$, ridge solves

\[\min_{\mathbf b}\left\{\|\mathbf y-X\mathbf b\|^2+\lambda\mathbf b^{ op}D\mathbf b ight\}, \qquad \widehat{ oldsymbol eta}_{\lambda} =(X^{ op}X+\lambda D)^{-1}X^{ op}\mathbf y, \qquad \lambda>0.\]
Penalizing all slopes makes this inverse well defined even with collinear slopes. Ridge trades bias for reduced variance; its fitted-value matrix is generally not an orthogonal projection. Lasso replaces the quadratic penalty by $\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{d-1} b_j $, which can set slopes exactly to zero and can have nonunique coefficients under collinearity. Penalties depend on predictor scales, so standardization and the convention for $\lambda$ matter. Classical OLS $t$ and $F$ formulas do not automatically apply to either penalized estimator.
entry.summary: Least squares, projection geometry, inference, and estimability

entry.title: A Conditional Expectation for Normal Variables

link.title: A Conditional Expectation for Normal Variables

entry.content:
Problem.

X and Y each have distribution $N(0,1)$, with correlation $\rho$. What is $\mathbb E[X\mid X+Y>0]$?

Solution.

1. The missing assumption

The normal marginals and correlation alone do not determine the answer. To obtain the usual formula, assume additionally that $X$ and $Y$ are jointly normal. First consider $-1<\rho\leq1$, and put

\[S=X+Y, \qquad S\sim N(0,\sigma_S^2), \qquad \sigma_S^2=2(1+\rho)>0.\]

2. Condition on the sum

Write $X=S/2+R$, where $R=(X-Y)/2$. Then

\[\mathbb E[R]=0, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(R,S) =\frac12\operatorname{Cov}(X-Y,X+Y) =\frac12\bigl(\operatorname{Var}(X)-\operatorname{Var}(Y)\bigr)=0.\]

Since $R$ and $S$ are jointly normal, zero covariance implies independence. This also covers $\rho=1$, when $R=0$ almost surely. Consequently,

\[\boxed{\mathbb E[X\mid S]=\frac S2.}\]

3. Normalize the truncated density

By symmetry, $\mathbb P(S>0)=1/2$. Conditioning on $S>0$ restricts the density to the positive half-line and divides by the probability of that half-line:

\[f_{S\mid S>0}(s) =\frac{f_S(s)}{\mathbb P(S>0)} =\frac{2}{\sigma_S\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-s^2/(2\sigma_S^2)}, \qquad s>0.\]

Thus the conditional mean is

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[S\mid S>0] &=\int_0^\infty s\frac{f_S(s)}{\mathbb P(S>0)}\,ds\\ &=\frac{2}{\sigma_S\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty s e^{-s^2/(2\sigma_S^2)}\,ds\\ &=\frac{2\sigma_S}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \left[-e^{-s^2/(2\sigma_S^2)}\right]_0^\infty =\sigma_S\sqrt{\frac2\pi}. \end{aligned}\]

Without the denominator $\mathbb P(S>0)$, the integral would give $\mathbb E[S\mathbf1_{{S>0}}]$, which is half the conditional mean. Averaging $\mathbb E[X\mid S]=S/2$ over $S>0$ now gives

\[\boxed{ \mathbb E[X\mid X+Y>0] =\frac12\mathbb E[S\mid S>0] =\sqrt{\frac{1+\rho}{\pi}}, \qquad -1<\rho\leq1. }\]

If $\rho=-1$, then $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=0$, so $X+Y=0$ almost surely. The conditioning event has probability zero, and the requested conditional expectation is undefined.

4. Why normal marginals are insufficient

Let $X\sim N(0,1)$, let $\varepsilon$ be an independent fair sign taking values $\pm1$, and set $Y=\varepsilon X$. Symmetry gives $Y\sim N(0,1)$, while

\[\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y) =\mathbb E[\varepsilon X^2] =\mathbb E[\varepsilon]\mathbb E[X^2]=0.\]

Here $X+Y>0$ occurs exactly when $\varepsilon=1$ and $X>0$, so

\[\mathbb E[X\mid X+Y>0] =\mathbb E[X\mid X>0] =\sqrt{\frac2\pi}.\]

Independent standard normals have the same marginals and correlation $0$, but give $1/\sqrt\pi$. Thus the joint distribution is needed to determine the answer.

entry.title: Traffic Clumps and Record Minima
entry.content:
Problem.

You have N cars that are all traveling in the same direction on an infinitely long one-lane highway. Unfortunately, they are all going at different speeds and cannot pass each other. Eventually, the cars will clump up in one or more traffic jams. In terms of N, what is the expected number of clumps of cars?

Example: 314682795.

Solution.

1. Clumps correspond to record minima

Index the cars from front to back, with distinct desired speeds $v_1,\ldots,v_N$. Assume finite initial gaps and a uniformly random ordering of the speeds; i.i.d. continuous speeds also satisfy the ordering assumption. Each car keeps its desired speed until it catches a slower clump, whose speed it then adopts.

Let $C_N$ be the eventual number of clumps, and define

\[m_0=+\infty, \qquad m_i=\min_{1\leq j\leq i}v_j.\]

Inductively, the rearmost clump among the first $i-1$ cars eventually travels at speed $m_{i-1}$. If $v_i<m_{i-1}$, car $i$ cannot catch any clump ahead and starts a new clump. If $v_i>m_{i-1}$, its positive relative speed and the finite gap ensure that it eventually joins the rearmost clump ahead. Hence the clump leaders are exactly the record minima:

\[I_i:=\mathbf1_{\{v_i<m_{i-1}\}}, \qquad I_1=1, \qquad C_N=\sum_{i=1}^N I_i.\]

For the example, read $3,1,4,6,8,2,7,9,5$ from front to back. Its record minima are $3$ and $1$, so there are two clumps: the first car, and a clump led by the car of speed $1$ containing every remaining car.

2. Take expectations

Under a uniformly random ordering, each of the first $i$ positions is equally likely to contain their minimum. Therefore

\[\mathbb P(I_i=1) =\mathbb P\!\left(v_i=\min_{1\leq j\leq i}v_j\right) =\frac1i.\]

Linearity of expectation gives

\[\boxed{ \mathbb E[C_N] =\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E[I_i] =\sum_{i=1}^N\frac1i =H_N. }\]

No independence assumption between the indicators is needed for this step.

entry.title: An Acute Triangle on a Circle

link.title: An Acute Triangle on a Circle

entry.content:
Problem.

Three points are chosen independently and uniformly on the circumference of a circle. What is the probability that they form an acute triangle?

Solution.

1. Translate the angle condition into a semicircle condition

Let $G_1,G_2,G_3$ be the angular lengths of the arcs between successive sampled points, so $G_1+G_2+G_3=2\pi$. By the inscribed-angle theorem, the triangle’s angles are $G_1/2,G_2/2,G_3/2$, in the corresponding opposite order. Hence

\[\text{the triangle is acute} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \max\{G_1,G_2,G_3\}<\pi.\]

A gap greater than $\pi$ leaves all three points on a complementary arc shorter than $\pi$, and conversely. Thus the triangle is obtuse exactly when its vertices lie in some open semicircle.

Coincident points and antipodal pairs have probability zero. Right triangles therefore have probability zero, and the acute-triangle probability is the complement of the semicircle probability.

2. Anchor the semicircle at a sampled point

Label the original sampled points $P_1,P_2,P_3$. For each $i$, let $A_i$ be the event that both other points lie in the clockwise open semicircle beginning at $P_i$. Conditional on $P_i$, each of the two other points independently falls in that semicircle with probability $1/2$. Hence

\[\mathbb P(A_i)=\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14.\]

If the points fit in an open semicircle, its first sampled point in clockwise order is an anchor for which $A_i$ holds. Conversely, each $A_i$ puts all three points in some open semicircle. Thus the semicircle event is $A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3$.

The events $A_i$ are pairwise disjoint. If both $A_i$ and $A_j$ held, the clockwise angular distance from $P_i$ to $P_j$ and the clockwise distance back from $P_j$ to $P_i$ would both be less than $\pi$. This is impossible because they sum to $2\pi$.

Consequently, the semicircle event has probability $\sum_{i=1}^3\mathbb P(A_i)=3/4$, and

\[\boxed{\mathbb P(\text{acute})=1-\frac34=\frac14.}\]

Related post. All Points in a Semicircle gives the general probability $N/2^{N-1}$ for $N$ independent uniform points. This problem uses its $N=3$ case and takes the complement.

entry.title: Three People at a Round Table

link.title: Three People at a Round Table

entry.content:
Problem.

Three people choose three distinct seats uniformly at random around a circular table with eight seats. What is the probability that at least two of them sit next to each other?

Solution.

Number the seats $1,\ldots,8$ clockwise, with seats $8$ and $1$ adjacent. There are $\binom83=56$ equally likely sets of three occupied seats, since each set allows the same $3!$ assignments of people. Let $N$ be the number of these sets with no adjacent occupied seats. The required probability is $1-N/56$.

To count $N$, temporarily mark one occupied seat as the starting point. Reading clockwise from it, let $g_1,g_2,g_3$ be the numbers of empty seats between successive occupied seats, including the gap back to the start. The five empty seats must form three nonempty gaps:

\[g_1+g_2+g_3=5, \qquad g_i\geq1.\]

Stars and bars gives $\binom{5-1}{3-1}=\binom42=6$ ordered gap triples. There are $8$ choices for the starting seat, and each starting seat and gap triple determines a configuration. This gives $8\binom42$ configurations with a marked starting seat.

Each occupied-seat set is counted exactly $3$ times, because any of its three occupied seats can be marked as the start. For example, the set ${1,3,5}$ is counted once starting at $1$, once at $3$, and once at $5$. Therefore,

\[N=\frac{8\binom42}{3}=16.\]

Taking the complement,

\[\boxed{ \mathbb P(\text{at least one adjacent pair}) =1-\frac{16}{56} =\frac57. }\]

Related post. The positive-gap count is an application of Stars and Bars – Empty and Nonempty Groups.

entry.title: Ants on a String
entry.content:
Problem.

500 ants are randomly put on a 1-foot string (independent uniform distribution for each ant between 0 and 1). Each ant randomly moves toward one end of the string (equal probability to the left or right) at constant speed of 1 foot/minute until it falls off at one end of the string. Also assume that the size of the ant is infinitely small. When two ants collide head-on, they both immediately change directions and keep on moving at 1 foot/min. What is the expected time for all ants to fall off the string?

Solution.

The key observation is that a collision is equivalent to exchanging labels. If we swap the two ants’ labels whenever they collide and reverse direction, each label continues moving in its original direction. The occupied positions and all departure times are unchanged. Thus, we may calculate the time until the string is empty by letting the ants pass straight through one another.

In this equivalent model, let $X_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$ be the initial position of ant $i$. Its departure time, measured in minutes, is

\[T_i= \begin{cases} X_i,&\text{if it initially moves left},\\ 1-X_i,&\text{if it initially moves right}. \end{cases}\]

For $0\leq t\leq1$,

\[\mathbb P(T_i\leq t) =\frac12\mathbb P(X_i\leq t) +\frac12\mathbb P(X_i\geq1-t) =\frac12t+\frac12t=t.\]

Therefore $T_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$. The initial positions and direction choices are independent across ants, so the departure times in this equivalent model are also independent.

All ants have fallen off when the last one leaves. Hence

\[T=\max_{1\leq i\leq500}T_i, \qquad \mathbb P(T\leq t) =\prod_{i=1}^{500}\mathbb P(T_i\leq t) =t^{500}, \quad 0\leq t\leq1.\]

Using the tail-integral formula for a nonnegative random variable,

\[\boxed{ \mathbb E[T] =\int_0^1\mathbb P(T>t)\,dt =\int_0^1(1-t^{500})\,dt =\frac{500}{501}\text{ minutes}. }\]

entry.title: Two Rows of Shopping Carts
entry.content:
Problem.

Two rows initially contain $5$ and $6$ shopping carts. Each customer chooses a row with probability $1/2$ and takes one cart. The customer later returns that cart to a row chosen independently, again with probability $1/2$ for each row. The next customer arrives only after the previous customer has returned the cart.

After each customer returns the cart, check whether either row is empty. What is the expected number of customers until this first happens?

Solution.

1. One time step per customer

Let the initial row sizes be $a,b\ge1$, with $N=a+b$. Define $X_n$ as the number of carts in the first row after the $n$-th customer has returned a cart, and set $X_0=a$. One unit of time is one complete customer visit.

For customer $n$, let $U_n$ indicate that the cart is taken from the first row and $V_n$ indicate that it is returned to the first row. The variables $U_n,V_n$ are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter $1/2$, independently across customers. Before the process stops,

\[X_{n+1}=X_n-U_{n+1}+V_{n+1}.\]

Thus, for an interior state $1\le i\le N-1$,

\[\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i) = \begin{cases} 1/4,&j=i-1,\\ 1/2,&j=i,\\ 1/4,&j=i+1,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\]

The four equally likely possibilities for one customer are:

Row used for taking Row used for returning Change in $X_n$
First First $0$
First Second $-1$
Second First $+1$
Second Second $0$

At every observation time the two rows together contain $N$ carts. Define the stopping time

\[T:=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in\{0,N\}\}.\]

The boundary states are absorbing. A temporary empty row while a customer is away does not stop the process: the check is made only after the return.

2. First-step recurrence

Write

\[e_i:=\mathbb E[T\mid X_0=i], \qquad 0\le i\le N.\]

Then $e_0=e_N=0$. From an interior state, one customer is served before the process either stops or continues from its new state. Therefore,

\[e_i =1+\frac14e_{i-1}+\frac12e_i+\frac14e_{i+1}, \qquad 1\le i\le N-1.\]

The constant $1$ counts one customer, including the customer whose completed visit first leaves a row empty. Rearranging gives

\[\boxed{ e_{i+1}-2e_i+e_{i-1}=-4, \qquad e_0=e_N=0. }\]

3. Solve the difference equation

Introduce the first differences

\[d_i:=e_i-e_{i-1}, \qquad i=1,\ldots,N.\]

The recurrence becomes

\[d_{i+1}-d_i=-4, \qquad i=1,\ldots,N-1,\]

so

\[d_i=d_1-4(i-1).\]

Using $e_0=0$ and summing the differences,

\[\begin{aligned} e_i &=\sum_{j=1}^{i}d_j\\ &=i\,d_1-4\sum_{j=1}^{i}(j-1)\\ &=i\,d_1-2i(i-1). \end{aligned}\]

The other boundary condition determines $d_1$:

\[0=e_N=N\,d_1-2N(N-1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_1=2(N-1).\]

Consequently,

\[\boxed{e_i=2i(N-i).}\]

For the original initial state, $N=11$ and $X_0=5$. Hence

\[\boxed{\mathbb E[T]=e_5=2\cdot5\cdot(11-5)=60\text{ customers}.}\]

More generally, the initial row sizes $(a,b)$ give $\mathbb E[T]=e_a=2ab$.

entry.title: HHT Before HTH – A Conditional Waiting Time

link.title: HHT Before HTH – A Conditional Waiting Time

entry.content:
Problem.

A fair coin is tossed independently until either $HHT$ or $HTH$ appears as three consecutive outcomes. Conditional on $HHT$ appearing first, what is the expected number of tosses?

Solution.

Let $T$ be the total number of tosses until either pattern first appears, and let $W$ be the event that $HHT$ appears before $HTH$. We seek $\mathbb E[T\mid W]$.

Record only the longest suffix of the observed tosses that matches an unfinished beginning of either target. The possible suffixes are $\varnothing,H,HH,HT$. For example, $HHH$ is recorded as $HH$, while $HTT$ is recorded as $\varnothing$. For a current suffix $s$, write $\mathbb P_s,\mathbb E_s$ for probability and expectation starting from that suffix, and let $\tau$ count the additional tosses until one target is completed. From $\varnothing$, $\tau=T$.

1. The probability that HHT appears first

Define

\[q_s:=\mathbb P_s(W), \qquad s\in\{\varnothing,H,HH,HT\}.\]

Conditioning on the next toss gives

\[\begin{aligned} q_\varnothing&=\tfrac12q_\varnothing+\tfrac12q_H,\\ q_H&=\tfrac12q_{HH}+\tfrac12q_{HT},\\ q_{HH}&=\tfrac12q_{HH}+\tfrac12,\\ q_{HT}&=\tfrac12q_\varnothing. \end{aligned}\]

In the third equation, a tail completes $HHT$; in the fourth, a head completes $HTH$ and contributes zero. Solving,

\[q_{HH}=1,\qquad q_H=q_\varnothing,\qquad q_{HT}=\frac12q_\varnothing,\]

and hence

\[q_\varnothing=\frac12+\frac14q_\varnothing.\]

Therefore,

\[\boxed{ q_\varnothing=q_H=\frac23,\qquad q_{HH}=1,\qquad q_{HT}=\frac13. }\]

2. The first moment restricted to successful outcomes

Define

\[m_s:=\mathbb E_s[\tau\,\mathbf1_W].\]

Its relation to the conditional expectation is

\[m_s=q_s\,\mathbb E_s[\tau\mid W], \qquad q_s=\mathbb P_s(W).\]

Starting from suffix $s$, let $\tau’$ be the number of tosses still needed after the next toss, with $\tau’=0$ if that toss completes a target. Then

\[\tau=1+\tau'.\]

Consequently,

\[\begin{aligned} m_s &=\mathbb E_s[(1+\tau')\mathbf1_W]\\ &=\underbrace{\mathbb E_s[\mathbf1_W]}_{q_s} +\mathbb E_s[\tau'\mathbf1_W]. \end{aligned}\]

Although the next toss certainly takes place, it contributes $1$ to $\tau\mathbf1_W$ only when $W$ occurs. Its expected contribution is therefore the success probability $q_s$.

Let $P_{sj}$ be the probability that the next toss leaves the unfinished suffix $j\in{\varnothing,H,HH,HT}$. Conditional on this outcome, the remaining weighted expectation is $m_j$; if a target is completed, there is no remaining contribution. Conditioning on the next suffix gives

\[m_s=q_s+\sum_jP_{sj}m_j.\]

Using the next-toss probabilities and $q_\varnothing=q_H=2/3$, $q_{HH}=1$, $q_{HT}=1/3$, we obtain

\[\begin{aligned} m_\varnothing&=\tfrac23+\tfrac12m_\varnothing+\tfrac12m_H,\\ m_H&=\tfrac23+\tfrac12m_{HH}+\tfrac12m_{HT},\\ m_{HH}&=1+\tfrac12m_{HH},\\ m_{HT}&=\tfrac13+\tfrac12m_\varnothing. \end{aligned}\]

Solving these equations gives

\[m_\varnothing=\frac{38}{9}.\]

Finally, by the definition of conditional expectation,

\[\boxed{ \mathbb E[T\mid W] =\frac{\mathbb E[T\mathbf1_W]}{\mathbb P(W)} =\frac{m_\varnothing}{q_\varnothing} =\frac{38/9}{2/3} =\frac{19}{3}. }\]
